==Problem 22==
Point <imath>E</imath> is the midpoint of side <imath>\overline{CD}</imath> in square <imath>ABCD,</imath> and <imath>\overline{BE}</imath> meets diagonal <imath>\overline{AC}</imath> at <imath>F.</imath> The area of quadrilateral <imath>AFED</imath> is <imath>45.</imath> What is the area of <imath>ABCD?</imath>

<asy>
size(5cm);
draw((0,0)--(6,0)--(6,6)--(0,6)--cycle);
draw((0,6)--(6,0)); draw((3,0)--(6,6));
label("$A$",(0,6),NW);
label("$B$",(6,6),NE);
label("$C$",(6,0),SE);
label("$D$",(0,0),SW);
label("$E$",(3,0),S);
label("$F$",(4,2),E);
</asy>

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 100 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 108 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 120 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 135 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 144</imath>

==Solution 1==
We can use analytic geometry for this problem.

Let us start by giving <imath>D</imath> the coordinate <imath>(0,0)</imath>, <imath>A</imath> the coordinate <imath>(0,1)</imath>, and so forth. <imath>\overline{AC}</imath> and <imath>\overline{EB}</imath> can be represented by the equations <imath>y=-x+1</imath> and <imath>y=2x-1</imath>, respectively. Solving for their intersection gives point <imath>F</imath> coordinates <imath>\left(\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}\right)</imath>. 

Now, we can see that <imath>\triangle</imath><imath>EFC</imath>’s area is simply <imath>\frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3}}{2}</imath> or <imath>\frac{1}{12}</imath>. This means that pentagon <imath>ABCEF</imath>’s area is <imath>\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{12}=\frac{7}{12}</imath> of the entire square, and it follows that quadrilateral <imath>AFED</imath>’s area is <imath>\frac{5}{12}</imath> of the square. 

The area of the square is then <imath>\frac{45}{\frac{5}{12}}=9\cdot12=\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 108}</imath>.

==Solution 2==

Let <imath>x</imath> be the sides of the square. <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> has half the area of the square.
<imath>\triangle FEC</imath> has base equal to half the square side length, and by AA Similarity with <imath>\triangle FBA</imath>, it has <imath>\frac{1}{1+2}= \frac{1}{3}</imath> the height, so has <imath>\dfrac1{12}</imath>th of the area of square(<imath>\dfrac1{2}</imath>*<imath>\dfrac1{2}</imath>*<imath>\dfrac1{3}</imath> according to the triangle area formula). Thus, the area of the quadrilateral is <imath>1-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{12}=\frac{5}{12}</imath> of the area of the square. We get <imath>\frac{1}{3}</imath> because since the side length ratio of <imath>EC</imath> to <imath>AB</imath> is 2, the area ratio would be <imath>4</imath>. Hence, <imath>\frac{1}{12}</imath> <imath>\cdot</imath> <imath>4 = \frac{1}{3}.</imath> 

The area of <imath>\triangle ADC</imath> is <imath>\frac{x \cdot x}{2}.</imath> Thus, the area of <imath>AFED</imath> equals to the area of <imath>\triangle ADC</imath> minus the area of <imath>\triangle FEC</imath>, which is <imath>\frac{1}{12}</imath> of <imath>x^2</imath> (the area of the square).

We can write the equation:
<imath>\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^2}{12} = 45.</imath>

Solving the equation, we get <imath>x=\sqrt{108}.</imath>

The area of the square is then <imath>\sqrt{108} \cdot \sqrt{108} =\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 108}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
Extend <imath>\overline{AD}</imath> and <imath>\overline{BE}</imath> to meet at <imath>X</imath>. Drop an altitude from <imath>F</imath> to <imath>\overline{CE}</imath> and call it <imath>h</imath>. Also, call <imath>\overline{CE}</imath> <imath>x</imath>. As stated before, we have <imath>\triangle ABF \sim \triangle CEF</imath>, so the ratio of their heights is in a <imath>1:2</imath> ratio, making the altitude from <imath>F</imath> to <imath>\overline{AB}</imath> <imath>2h</imath>. Note that this means that the side of the square is <imath>3h</imath>. In addition, <imath>\triangle XDE \sim \triangle XAB</imath> by AA Similarity in a <imath>1:2</imath> ratio. This means that the square's side length is <imath>2x</imath>, making <imath>3h=2x</imath>.

Now, note that <imath>[ADEF]=[XAB]-[XDE]-[ABF]</imath>. We have <imath>[\triangle XAB]=(4x)(2x)/2=4x^2,</imath> <imath>[\triangle XDE]=(x)(2x)/2=x^2,</imath> and <imath>[\triangle ABF]=(2x)(2h)/2=(2x)(4x/3)/2=4x^2/3.</imath> Subtracting makes <imath>[ADEF]=4x^2-x^2-4x^2/3=5x^2/3.</imath> We are given that <imath>[ADEF]=45,</imath> so <imath>5x^2/3=45 \Rightarrow x^2=27.</imath> Therefore, <imath>x= 3 \sqrt{3},</imath> so our answer is <imath>(2x)^2=4x^2=4(27)=\boxed{\textbf{(B) }108}.</imath>

==Solution 4==

Solution with Cartesian and Barycentric Coordinates:

We start with the following:

Claim: Given a square <imath>ABCD</imath>, let <imath>E</imath> be the midpoint of <imath>\overline{DC}</imath> and let <imath>BE\cap AC = F</imath>. Then <imath>\frac {AF}{FC}=2</imath>.

Proof: We use Cartesian coordinates. Let <imath>D</imath> be the origin, <imath>A=(0,1),C=(0,1),B=(1,1)</imath>. We have that <imath>\overline{AC}</imath> and <imath>\overline{EB}</imath> are governed by the equations <imath>y=-x+1</imath> and <imath>y=2x-1</imath>, respectively. Solving, <imath>F=\left(\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}\right)</imath>. The result follows. <imath>\square</imath>

Now, we apply Barycentric Coordinates w.r.t. <imath>\triangle ACD</imath>. We let <imath>A=(1,0,0),D=(0,1,0),C=(0,0,1)</imath>. Then <imath>E=(0,\tfrac 12,\tfrac 12),F=(\tfrac 13,0,\tfrac 23)</imath>. 

In the barycentric coordinate system, the area formula is <imath>[XYZ]=\begin{vmatrix} x_{1} &y_{1}  &z_{1} \\ x_{2} &y_{2}  &z_{2} \\   x_{3}& y_{3} & z_{3} \end{vmatrix}\cdot [ABC]</imath> where <imath>\triangle XYZ</imath> is a random triangle and <imath>\triangle ABC</imath> is the reference triangle. Using this, we find that<cmath>\frac{[FEC]}{[ACD]}=\begin{vmatrix} 0&0&1\\ 0&\tfrac 12&\tfrac 12\\ \tfrac 13&0&\tfrac 23 \end{vmatrix}=\frac16.</cmath> Let <imath>[FEC]=x</imath> so that <imath>[ACD]=45+x</imath>. Then, we have <imath>\frac{x}{x+45}=\frac 16 \Rightarrow x=9</imath>, so the answer is <imath>2(45+9)=\boxed{108}</imath>.

Note: Please do not learn Barycentric Coordinates for the AMC 8.

==Solution 5 (easier)==

<imath>\triangle ABF \sim \triangle FEC</imath>, and the bases <imath>AB</imath> and <imath>EC</imath> are in the ratio <imath>2:1</imath>, so <imath>\frac{[\triangle ABF]}{[\triangle FEC]}=\left(\frac{2}{1}\right)^2=\frac{4}{1}</imath>, and <imath>[\triangle ABF]=4\cdot[\triangle FEC]</imath>

It is obvious that <imath>[AFED]+[\triangle FEC]=45+[\triangle FEC]=\frac{1}{2}\cdot[ABCD]</imath>

and <imath>[AFED]+[\triangle ABF]=45+4\cdot[\triangle FEC]=\frac{3}{4}\cdot[ABCD]</imath>

Solving the two equations we get <imath>[ABCD]=\boxed{\textbf{(B)}108}</imath>

==Solution 6 (Similar to 5)==
Since we know that point <imath>E</imath> is the midpoint of square with area <imath>4x^2</imath> (Side length of <imath>2x</imath>) we can easily tell that <imath>\overline{EC}</imath> is equal to <imath>\overline{DE}</imath>. This especially helpful when we realize that <imath>\triangle ECF\sim \triangle ABF</imath>. Our setup is over, it is time to solve! 

We can label the area of <imath>\triangle ECF</imath> as <imath>a</imath>, which means that <imath>\triangle ABF</imath> has an area of <imath>4a</imath> (This is because the width and height doubles which means the area is four times that of <imath>\triangle ECF</imath>). Since we know that the area of quadrilateral <imath>ADEF</imath> is <imath>45</imath>, this means that <imath>45+a=2x^2</imath>(half of the area due to diagonal). 

Now we should find the area of trapezoid <imath>ABED</imath>. Since the bases are <imath>x</imath> and <imath>2x</imath> and the height is also <imath>2x</imath>, we can plug these values into the formula for the area of the trapezoid(<imath>\tfrac{b_{1}+b_{2}}{2}\cdot h</imath>), and we will get the area as <imath>3x^2</imath> which is equal to <imath>45+4a</imath>. We now have our two equations: <imath>45+a=2x^2</imath> and <imath>45+4a=3x^3</imath>.

We can now multiply the first equation by four so we can easily subtract the variable <imath>a</imath>. Doing this we acquire <imath>180+4a=8x^2</imath>, and when we subtract both equations, we get <imath>135=5x^2</imath>. Remember, if we want to find the area, we have to look for <imath>4x^2</imath>, which is <imath>\frac{135}{5} \cdot 4</imath>. 135 divided by 5 is 27, and 27 times 4 is  <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}108}</imath>.

==Solution 7 (Basic Concepts)==
Set the length of <imath>EC</imath> to <imath>x</imath>. We now will proceed to find the altitude of triangle <imath>FEC</imath> if we consider line <imath>EC</imath> to be the base.

Notice that <imath>\triangle FEC</imath> and <imath>\triangle FAB</imath> are similar. Since the ratio of their bases is <imath>1:2</imath>, respectively, we can now set up a proportion: <imath>\dfrac{x}{y}=\dfrac{2x}{2x-y}</imath>. Cross-multiplying and simplifying gives the equation <imath>2x=3y</imath>, or <imath>y=\dfrac{2}{3}x</imath>. From there, we can see that the area of <imath>\triangle FEC = \dfrac{1}{3}x^2</imath>.

Now, we subtract the area of <imath>\triangle FEC</imath> from <imath>\triangle ADC</imath> and set it equal to <imath>45</imath>. Our equation then becomes <imath>2x^2-\dfrac{1}{3}x^2=45</imath>, which upon solving for <imath>x</imath> yields <imath>x=3\sqrt{3}</imath>, so the side length of the square is <imath>6\sqrt{3}</imath>, and squaring <imath>6\sqrt{3}</imath> gives <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}108}</imath>.

~ BlueAnglerfish42
